meta.compiled_by: Claude (research subagent) for Report AI; research only, no WordPress access
meta.conventions: confidence: HIGH = primary source opened and figure seen; MEDIUM = secondary source or web-search summary only (verified_how says which). DERIVED in verified_how = Report AI computed the figure. Dates are ISO (YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD); 'date' is the figure's as-of/publication date. value null = qualitative finding. Leaderboard positions are 1-based. Vendor technical reports (Prior Labs, Amazon, LimiX, Meta) are self-reported claims.

facts.sentence: TabPFN v2 was published by Hollmann, Müller, Purucker and colleagues (University of Freiburg / Prior Labs) in Nature volume 637, pages 319-326, in January 2025, under the title "Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model".
facts.verified_how: Full citation (volume, issue, pages, author list) read in the reference list of the TabPFN-3 technical report on arxiv.org (ref [17]) and in the PriorLabs/TabPFN GitHub README. nature.com itself was not reachable from this session.
facts.note: nature.com, PubMed and PMC are blocked in this session; citation verified via two independent primary-adjacent documents.

facts.sentence: According to the abstract of Hollmann et al. (Nature, January 2025), TabPFN outperforms all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples "by a wide margin".
facts.source: Hollmann et al., Nature 2025 (abstract), quoted in Zhang et al. arXiv:2505.20003
facts.verified_how: Quote of the Nature abstract read on the arXiv abstract page of Zhang, Tan, Tian & Li (2505.20003); also Section 1 of the TabPFN-2.5 report (arXiv 2511.08667) says v2 was 'a practical model for datasets up to 10,000 samples'.
facts.note: The Nature page itself was not opened (blocked).

facts.sentence: Prior Labs' TabPFN-2.5 technical report (arXiv, November 2025) lists TabPFN v2's recommended maximum as 10,000 rows and 500 features.
facts.source: Grinsztajn et al., TabPFN-2.5 technical report, Table 1
facts.verified_how: Read Table 1 of the arXiv HTML version.

facts.sentence: The Nature abstract (Hollmann et al., January 2025) states that in a classification setting TabPFN in 2.8 seconds outperforms an ensemble of the strongest baselines tuned for 4 hours.
facts.verified_how: Seen only in a web-search summary of the PubMed abstract (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39780007). The primary page could not be opened from this session.
facts.note: Widely repeated; wording appears consistent across sources, but confirm on nature.com before publishing as HIGH. Note the comparison is a classification-setting claim, not a universal one.

facts.sentence: TabPFN v2 was pretrained only on synthetic datasets generated from a prior based on structural causal models; Wikipedia, citing the Nature paper, puts the number at about 130 million synthetic datasets.
facts.source: Wikipedia 'TabPFN' (citing Hollmann et al. 2025); TabPFN-3 report Sec. 2.5 for the SCM prior
facts.verified_how: SCM prior confirmed in TabPFN-3 report Sec. 2.5 ('trained on synthetically generated data based on our Structural Causal Model (SCM) prior'). The 130 million figure was seen only on Wikipedia.
facts.note: CONFLICT: a web-search summary of the University of Freiburg press release (Jan 2025) gives '100 million' synthetic datasets. Do not publish either number until the Nature Methods section is checked.

facts.sentence: Prior Labs' TabPFN-3 technical report (arXiv, May 2026) states that the open-source tabpfn package had passed 3.2 million PyPI downloads and the Nature paper had been cited in over 1,000 papers, both as of 8 May 2026.
facts.verified_how: Read in arXiv HTML Sec. 4.1 and its footnote (Google Scholar and pepy.tech, accessed May 8, 2026).
facts.note: Vendor-reported. The TabPFN-2.5 report (Nov 2025) gave 'almost 400' citations in 10 months and 2,000,000+ PyPI downloads.

facts.sentence: Prior Labs' TabPFN-2.5, described in an arXiv technical report first posted on 11 November 2025, is built for datasets with up to 50,000 rows and 2,000 features, a 20-fold increase in data cells over TabPFN v2.
facts.source: Grinsztajn et al., TabPFN-2.5 technical report (arXiv 2511.08667)
facts.verified_how: Read abstract and Table 1 on arxiv.org; same limits on the Hugging Face model card Prior-Labs/tabpfn_2_5.

facts.sentence: The TabPFN-2.5 report (Prior Labs, November 2025) claims a 100% win rate against default XGBoost on small and medium classification datasets (up to 10,000 rows and 500 features), 87% on larger datasets (up to 100,000 rows) and 85% for regression.
facts.verified_how: Read on arXiv abstract page.
facts.note: Comparison is against XGBoost with DEFAULT hyperparameters, not tuned XGBoost.

facts.sentence: The TabPFN-2.5 weights on Hugging Face are released under the 'TABPFN-2.5 License v1.1' (last revised 9 December 2025), which permits only non-commercial use and requires a separate commercial licence for any commercial or production use.
facts.verified_how: Opened the LICENSE file; Section 2(b) 'Non-Commercial Use Only'.
facts.note: The TabPFN-2.5 report (Sec. 6) refers to 'License v1.0'; the current file is v1.1.

facts.sentence: TabPFN v2 weights (Hugging Face Prior-Labs/TabPFN-v2-clf) are released under the Prior Labs License v1.1 (May 2025), a derivative of Apache 2.0 with an added Section 10 requiring products that use the weights to display "Built with PriorLabs-TabPFN".
facts.verified_how: Opened LICENSE.txt (the file is LICENSE.txt, not LICENSE). Model card header: 'License: priorlabs-1-1'.
facts.note: Section 10 also requires distributed models trained/distilled from the weights or outputs to have names beginning with 'TabPFN'. Internal benchmarking without external communication does not trigger attribution.

facts.sentence: As of November 2026 the PriorLabs/TabPFN GitHub README states that the TabPFN-2.5, 2.6, 3, 3.5 and 3.5-Fast weights are released under non-commercial licences, while the code is Apache 2.0 and the TabPFN-2 weights remain Apache 2.0 with an attribution requirement.
facts.verified_how: Downloaded README.md from raw.githubusercontent.com (main branch) on 2026-11-15.

facts.sentence: The TabPFN-3.5 weights are licensed under the 'TABPFN-3.5 License v1.0' (last revised 9 September 2026), a non-commercial licence requiring a separate commercial licence for production use.
facts.verified_how: Opened the LICENSE file.

facts.sentence: Prior Labs' TabPFN-3 technical report (arXiv, first posted 13 May 2026) says the model scales to 1 million training rows, is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and beats 8-hour-tuned gradient-boosted-tree baselines on datasets up to 1 million rows and 200 features.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract page (v3, 3 Nov 2026).
facts.note: Abstract also claims TabPFN-3 is up to 20x faster than TabPFN-2.5.

facts.sentence: As of November 2026, Prior Labs' default model TabPFN-3.5 (technical report first posted 15 September 2026; weights file dated 2026-09-09) accepts up to 1,000,000 rows and 20,000 features according to the PriorLabs/TabPFN README.
facts.source: PriorLabs/TabPFN README; TabPFN-3.5 technical report arXiv 2609.17895
facts.verified_how: README read directly; arXiv abstract page opened for date and claims.
facts.note: Wikipedia says the recommended maximum is 6,000 features with up to 20,000 possible using more estimators; the README says 'accept up to'. On CPU the README caps TabPFN-3/3.5 at 5,000 samples by default.

facts.sentence: Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (arXiv July 2022; NeurIPS 2022) benchmarked tree-based models against deep learning on 45 tabular datasets and found that tree-based models such as XGBoost and random forests remain state-of-the-art on medium-sized data of about 10,000 samples.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract and HTML full text (Sec. 3.1, 3.2).
facts.note: Training sets were truncated to 10,000 samples for the main 'medium-sized' regime; a secondary 'large' regime truncated at 50,000 (Appendix A.2.2). The paper's per-setting dataset counts (15+19+7+14) sum to more than 45 because some datasets appear in several settings.

facts.sentence: Grinsztajn et al. (2022) give three reasons neural networks lag trees on tabular data: neural networks are biased towards overly smooth solutions, MLP-like networks are hurt more by uninformative features, and tabular data are not invariant to rotation, so learners should not be either.
facts.verified_how: Section headings read in arXiv HTML.
facts.note: The abstract restates these as three design challenges: be robust to uninformative features, preserve the orientation of the data, and easily learn irregular functions.

facts.sentence: Grinsztajn et al. (2022) released raw results including every point of a 20,000-compute-hour hyperparameter search for each learner.
facts.verified_how: Read abstract.

facts.sentence: The Grinsztajn et al. paper appeared at NeurIPS 2022 in the Datasets and Benchmarks track.
facts.verified_how: Web-search results showed the nips.cc poster page and a proceedings file named '...-Supplemental-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.pdf'; proceedings.neurips.cc and openreview.net were blocked.

facts.sentence: The Hugging Face dataset inria-soda/tabular-benchmark packages the Grinsztajn et al. (2022) benchmark as 59 CSV files in four task folders: 16 numerical-feature classification, 7 mixed-feature classification, 19 numerical regression and 17 mixed-feature regression.
facts.verified_how: Downloaded README.md (dataset card) and counted data_files entries per folder. The LeoGrin/tabular-benchmark GitHub README links this Hugging Face dataset.
facts.note: The card lists 16 numeric classification datasets in its table though the paper text mentions 15; several datasets (e.g. covertype, electricity, house_sales) appear in more than one folder. The card states no licence.

facts.sentence: Datasets in the Grinsztajn benchmark had to have at least 4 features and 3,000 samples, a feature-to-sample ratio below 1/10, and were dropped as 'too easy' if a simple linear model or single tree scored within 5% of both a default ResNet and a default HistGradientBoosting model.
facts.source: arXiv 2207.08815 Sec. 3.1; Hugging Face dataset card
facts.verified_how: Read in both the arXiv HTML and the HF dataset card.
facts.note: Relevance for our benchmark: the 'too easy' filter deliberately removes datasets where logistic regression is near the best, which depresses linear-model results relative to everyday data.

facts.sentence: McElfresh et al. (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track) compared 19 algorithms on 176 tabular datasets, which the authors described as the largest tabular data analysis to date.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract (v4, July 2024; venue stated on page).

facts.sentence: McElfresh et al. (2023) found that the neural-net-versus-boosted-tree debate is overemphasised: for many datasets the gap is negligible, or light hyperparameter tuning of a GBDT matters more than the choice between model families.
facts.verified_how: Read abstract.

facts.sentence: McElfresh et al. (2023) report that GBDTs handle skewed or heavy-tailed feature distributions and other dataset irregularities much better than neural networks, while TabPFN (v1) performed best on average even when trained on only 3,000 randomly sampled points.
facts.verified_how: Read abstract.
facts.note: This is TabPFN v1 (2022), not the Nature v2 model.

facts.sentence: The TabZilla Benchmark Suite released by McElfresh et al. (2023) contains the 36 hardest datasets from their study.
facts.verified_how: Read abstract.

facts.sentence: Shwartz-Ziv and Armon (arXiv June 2021; Information Fusion 2022) found that XGBoost outperformed recently proposed deep tabular models on the datasets tested, including those used in the deep models' own papers, needed much less tuning, and that an ensemble of deep models plus XGBoost beat XGBoost alone.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract page (v2, 23 Nov 2021).
facts.note: Journal details (Information Fusion vol. 81, pp. 84-90, 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.inffus.2021.11.011) seen only in web-search results: MEDIUM. The abstract does not state the number of datasets.

facts.sentence: TabArena (Erickson et al., arXiv June 2025; NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks spotlight) is a continuously maintained 'living' benchmark that curated 51 datasets from 1,053 datasets used in 14 earlier benchmarks.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract and HTML Sec. 2.2.
facts.note: Datasets must have 500 to 250,000 training samples. The live leaderboard (Nov 2026) still uses 51 datasets in its default view (n_datasets.json).

facts.sentence: TabArena ranks models by Elo, with the default RandomForest configuration fixed at 1,000 and a 400-point gap corresponding to a 10-to-1 (about 91%) expected win rate.
facts.verified_how: Read Sec. 2.3; confirmed RandomForest (default) = 1000.0 in the live leaderboard CSV.

facts.sentence: The TabArena paper (2025) found that gradient-boosted trees remain strong on practical datasets but deep learning methods have caught up under larger time budgets with ensembling, and that foundation models excel on smaller datasets.
facts.verified_how: Read abstract.

facts.sentence: On TabArena's live leaderboard (default view: single models, 51 datasets, data regenerated 11 November 2026), the top five entries are NVIDIA's Kumo-Tabular (Elo 1971), LimiX-2 (1959), Kumo-Tabular-Medium (1909), Neuralk-AI's Seldon (1903) and Prior Labs' TabPFN-3.5 (1868), all tabular foundation models run with default settings.
facts.source: TabArena leaderboard (Hugging Face Space TabArena/leaderboard, v0.1.9.18, commit e0723ee)
facts.verified_how: Downloaded data/entrants_models/imputation_yes/splits_all/tasks_all/datasets_all/website_leaderboard.csv (the default view per api.py) on 2026-11-15; commit dated 2026-11-11.
facts.note: Confidence intervals overlap heavily (Kumo-Tabular +160/-99; LimiX-2 +130/-83), so the top-5 order is not statistically settled. LimiX-2 carries a leaderboard LEAKAGE WARNING (test data proven to have leaked into training on the blood-transfusion-service-center and diabetes datasets; tabarena issue #648). 3 of the top 5 (LimiX-2, Seldon, TabPFN-3.5) are marked non-commercial on the leaderboard; NVIDIA's Kumo-Tabular and Kumo-Tabular-Medium (OpenMDW-1.1) are marked commercial-use. LimiX-2 is listed under 'Stable AI & Tsinghua University'.

facts.sentence: In TabArena's default leaderboard view of 11 November 2026, the top 21 of 108 entries are tabular foundation models; the best non-foundation entry is the TabM-A neural network (tuned and ensembled, Elo 1517, 22nd), and the best tree model is LightGBM tuned and ensembled (Elo 1411, 32nd).
facts.verified_how: Counted from the downloaded CSV.
facts.note: Positions are 1-based; the CSV '#' column is 0-based.

facts.sentence: On TabArena's default leaderboard (11 November 2026), classic models rank far below: tuned-and-ensembled CatBoost scores Elo 1402, XGBoost 1360, RandomForest 1172, k-nearest neighbours 993 and linear models 990, against 1971 for the leader.
facts.verified_how: Read from CSV.
facts.note: Default-hyperparameter versions: CatBoost 1362, XGBoost 1208, LightGBM 1183, RandomForest 1000, Linear 862, KNN 635. No Naive Bayes, SVM or single decision tree is on the leaderboard.

facts.sentence: Successive TabPFN releases climb TabArena's default leaderboard (11 November 2026): TabPFN v2 default scores Elo 1251 (with 35% of runs imputed), TabPFN-2.6 1583, TabPFN-3 1631 and TabPFN-3.5 1868.
facts.verified_how: Read from CSV.
facts.note: 'Imputed' means the model could not run on some datasets (e.g. v2's 10k-row limit) and a default RandomForest result was substituted; this penalises v2.

facts.sentence: Ye et al.'s TALENT benchmark (arXiv July 2024, revised November 2025) covers more than 300 tabular datasets and finds that ensembling helps both tree and neural methods, gradient-boosted trees remain strong baselines, and recent pretrained tabular models match or beat them on many tasks.
facts.source: Ye, Liu, Cai, Zhou & Zhan, arXiv 2407.00956
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract (v4).
facts.note: Also defines TALENT-tiny (45 datasets).

facts.sentence: TabICL (Qu, Holzmüller, Varoquaux & Le Morvan, ICML 2025) was pretrained on synthetic datasets of up to 60,000 samples, handles up to 500,000 samples, and on 53 datasets with more than 10,000 samples outperformed both TabPFN v2 and CatBoost.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract.
facts.note: Evaluated on 200 TALENT classification datasets; up to 10x faster than TabPFN v2.

facts.sentence: Mitra-v2 (listed by TabArena as an Amazon model; arXiv 3 September 2026) is a 77-million-parameter tabular foundation model trained only on synthetic data and released under Apache-2.0; its authors report TabArena results comparable to the 1.6-billion-parameter TabFM.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract.
facts.note: On the live TabArena leaderboard (11 Nov 2026) Mitra-v2 default sits at Elo 1769 (11th). The arXiv abstract page does not state affiliation; the TabArena leaderboard lists the organisation as Amazon.

facts.sentence: LimiX-2 (arXiv 15 September 2026, 60 authors led by Xingxuan Zhang and Peng Cui) is pretrained with context-conditional masked modelling on synthetic structural-causal-model data and claims to beat existing tabular foundation models on TabArena, TALENT and BCCO.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract.
facts.note: TabArena flags LimiX-2 with a test-data leakage warning (see tabarena-lb-top).

facts.sentence: Wolpert's 1996 no-free-lunch theorems for supervised learning (Neural Computation, vol. 8, pp. 1341-1390) show that, averaged uniformly over all possible target functions, no learning algorithm has lower expected off-training-set error than any other, so any advantage must come from assumptions that match the problem.
facts.source: Wolpert, 'The Lack of A Priori Distinctions between Learning Algorithms', Neural Computation 8(7), DOI 10.1162/neco.1996.8.7.1341
facts.verified_how: Citation details read on Wikipedia ('No free lunch theorem' and 'No free lunch in search and optimization'); the paper itself (MIT Press) was not opened. The statement is a standard summary.
facts.note: Wikipedia notes critics argue NFL has little practical relevance because real-world problems are not uniformly distributed; do not use NFL to claim 'all models are equally good in practice'.

facts.sentence: Kaggle's 2022 Machine Learning and Data Science Survey, its sixth annual edition, collected 23,997 responses from 173 countries in September 2022.
facts.source: Kaggle 2022 ML & DS Survey (raw responses file)
facts.verified_how: 23,997 data rows counted in kaggle_survey_2022_responses.csv (copy in github.com/AlexanderVeshniakov/Educational_project_2, commit 9c427b0, sha256 7475cfa7...). 173 countries and 'sixth annual' from web-search summaries (MEDIUM).
facts.note: kaggle.com was not reachable; the CSV is a third-party mirror of Kaggle's official file. Most recent edition we found; we could not confirm whether any later edition exists.

facts.sentence: In Kaggle's 2022 survey, 71.5% of the 15,864 respondents who answered the algorithm question said they regularly use linear or logistic regression, 59.1% decision trees or random forests, 37.9% convolutional neural networks, 34.7% gradient boosting machines and 13.8% transformer networks.
facts.source: Kaggle 2022 ML & DS Survey, Q18 (Report AI calculation from raw responses)
facts.verified_how: DERIVED: Report AI tabulated Q18 'Which of the following ML algorithms do you use on a regular basis?' from the mirrored raw CSV. Denominator = respondents selecting at least one option (incl. 'None') = 15,864. As a share of all 23,997 respondents: 47.2 / 39.1 / 25.0 / 22.9 / 9.2.
facts.note: Other options: Bayesian approaches 23.1%, dense NNs/MLPs 21.9%, RNNs 21.8%, GNNs 9.0%, autoencoders 7.8%, GANs 7.3%, evolutionary 5.2%, None 8.4%. Kaggle's own published report may use a different denominator - check before publishing; label DERIVED.

facts.sentence: Facebook's 2014 paper 'Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook' (He et al., ADKDD 2014) combined boosted decision trees with logistic regression and reported that the hybrid beat either method alone by more than 3%.
facts.source: He et al., ADKDD 2014 (Meta research publication page)
facts.verified_how: Seen in web-search summary of the Meta/Facebook research publication page; Meta pages blocked from this session.
facts.note: The paper's headline lesson is that having the right features (historical user/ad information) matters most. Scale cited in summaries: 750M+ daily active users, 1M+ active advertisers (unverified).

facts.sentence: Google's 'Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations' (Covington, Adams & Sargin, RecSys 2016, Boston) describes a two-stage system: a deep candidate-generation network that narrows the video corpus, followed by a separate deep ranking network.
facts.verified_how: Abstract phrases ('a deep candidate generation model and then describe a separate deep ranking model') seen in web-search summary of research.google pages; research.google blocked.

facts.sentence: Twitter's open-sourced recommendation code (March 2023) describes the For You 'heavy ranker' as a neural network (a parallel MaskNet) that predicts the probability of ten engagement types, combined by a weighted sum in which, as of 5 April 2023, a predicted report carried weight -369 and a predicted like +0.5.
facts.verified_how: Read README from raw.githubusercontent.com.
facts.note: Weights multiply predicted probabilities, not raw counts (see x-2026-weights note).

facts.sentence: Twitter's engineering blog of 31 March 2023 said the For You pipeline pulls about 1,500 candidate tweets per request and ranks them with a roughly 48-million-parameter neural network.
facts.verified_how: 48M seen in a search snippet attributed to the official blog; 1,500 seen only in secondary write-ups (Hootsuite, SwirlAI). blog.x.com blocked.
facts.note: The GitHub READMEs confirm the light ranker / heavy ranker split and that ~50% of posts come from the in-network search-index source, but not the 1,500 or 48M figures.

facts.sentence: X's current open-source For You repository (xai-org/x-algorithm, updated through November 2026) says posts are ranked by a transformer model called Phoenix, which also uses a transformer two-tower model for retrieval; earlier releases shipped a sample transformer ported from xAI's Grok-1.
facts.verified_how: Read README files from raw.githubusercontent.com; latest commit 2026-11-14.
facts.note: First public release date (reported as 20 January 2026) seen only in secondary sources: MEDIUM. The README itself does not use the word 'Grok' except in the Phoenix note about earlier releases.

facts.sentence: X's For You README (update of 14 August 2026) warns that action weights scale each viewer's predicted probability of an action, so a report weighted 468 times a like does not mean one report cancels 468 likes.
facts.verified_how: Read README.
facts.note: Useful debunk of a commonly repeated misreading.

facts.sentence: ByteDance's Monolith paper (arXiv September 2022; ORSUM workshop at RecSys 2022) describes a real-time recommendation training system with a collisionless embedding table that updates models from user feedback online and is deployed in the BytePlus Recommend product.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract.
facts.note: The abstract names BytePlus Recommend, not TikTok. Do not write 'TikTok's algorithm is Monolith' without a primary source.

facts.sentence: Meta's 'Actions Speak Louder than Words' paper (Zhai et al., ICML 2024) reports that a 1.5-trillion-parameter generative recommender built on its HSTU transformer architecture improved online A/B-test metrics by 12.4% and was deployed on multiple surfaces of a platform with billions of users.
facts.verified_how: Read arXiv abstract.
facts.note: HSTU is reported as 5.3x-15.2x faster than FlashAttention2-based Transformers on 8,192-length sequences.

facts.sentence: Google said in October 2019 that its BERT transformer model would help Search understand about one in ten English-language searches in the United States.
facts.source: Google (Pandu Nayak), 'Understanding searches better than ever before', The Keyword blog
facts.verified_how: Seen in web-search summaries of TechCrunch and Fortune coverage quoting Google; blog.google not reachable.

facts.sentence: The first scholarly publication applying a naive Bayes classifier to spam filtering was Sahami, Dumais, Heckerman and Horvitz's 'A Bayesian approach to filtering junk e-mail' at the AAAI-98 Workshop on Learning for Text Categorization in 1998.
facts.source: Sahami et al., AAAI-98 workshop (via Wikipedia 'Naive Bayes spam filtering')
facts.verified_how: Read on Wikipedia; original paper not opened.
facts.note: Paul Graham's essay 'A Plan for Spam' (August 2002) popularised Bayesian filtering; date from Wikipedia (MEDIUM).

facts.sentence: Google said in February 2019 that its machine-learning and rules-based protections block more than 99.9% of spam, phishing and malware in Gmail, and that adding TensorFlow models blocked about 100 million additional spam messages a day.
facts.source: Google Workspace blog (Neil Kumaran), 'Ridding Gmail of 100 million more spam messages with TensorFlow'
facts.verified_how: Seen in web-search summary of the Google Workspace blog and press coverage; Google pages blocked.
facts.note: Self-reported by Google, not independently audited. Earlier claim: May 2017, ML gives '99.9% detection accuracy' for spam/phishing (Wikipedia citing TechCrunch, 31 May 2017).

facts.sentence: Logistic regression is described as the most popular statistical technique for building credit scorecards, predicting a binary outcome of default or no default.
facts.verified_how: Read Wikipedia wikitext; cites a 2015 University of Tartu thesis. No regulator or central-bank primary source reachable for this exact claim.
facts.note: Weak sourcing - use as context only, or replace with the Bank of England/FCA 2022 ML survey or Fed SR 11-7 once those hosts are reachable.

facts.sentence: A BIS working paper by Gambacorta, Huang, Qiu and Wang (No. 834, December 2019) found that a Chinese fintech's machine-learning credit model using non-traditional data predicted losses and defaults better than traditional bank models when credit supply was hit by a negative shock.
facts.verified_how: Read the BIS abstract page.
facts.note: The advantage shrinks for borrowers with longer credit histories. The abstract does not give accuracy/AUC figures.

facts.sentence: The Bank of England and FCA's 2022 survey 'Machine learning in UK financial services' found that 72% of responding firms were using or developing ML applications.
facts.source: Bank of England & FCA, Machine learning in UK financial services (2022)
facts.verified_how: Seen only in a web-search summary; bankofengland.co.uk not reachable. Summary also says tree-based models, regression and neural networks were the most common methods.
facts.note: The report says its sample is not representative of all UK financial services.

facts.sentence: Report AI could not locate or verify the short video 'Learn Software While You Sleep' captioned '13 machine learning models in 60 seconds', nor identify the dataset behind its accuracy chart (TabPFN 79.5%, neural network 74.0%, random forest 73.5%, Naive Bayes 42.1%).
facts.source: Report AI search (web search; YouTube not reachable from research environment)
facts.verified_how: Four web searches (exact title, caption phrase, exact accuracy figures) returned no match; youtube.com was blocked so platform search was impossible.
facts.note: Do not attribute the figures to any dataset or paper. The chart shows 9 models although the caption says 13. The owner may be able to supply the URL.
